posts.title: Installation concurrency when Windows has a mutex but not a queue
posts.description: Windows does not queue GUI or CLI installs across process trees—agents hit MSI 1618, custom EXE races, and package-manager exit codes. What exists, what we fake in orchestration, and what a real serialization API would need.
posts.html:
Agents that provision their own toolchains assume “install X” is a safe verb. On Windows it is often a bounce: a second workflow starts a setup while another still owns the machine’s install path, and the OS answers with a modal error, exit code 1618, or a silent file/registry race—not a ticket in a queue.

This piece is the Windows half of a diptych with Installation concurrency when Linux locks wait—or don’t. Read them together: same agentic pressure, different OS traditions, different places the fix can land.

Practitioner short form (agent-host mutex rule, no OS treatise): OS install concurrency on the docs hub.

The short answer

Windows has no native OS-level queue or signaling system for GUI- or CLI-driven software installation that independent process trees can share. Concurrent installer invocations do not line up behind a job scheduler. They fail fast on a shared lock, collide outside any lock, or serialize only inside one package-manager process that still shells out into the same contested world.

What actually serializes today

Windows Installer (MSI / msiexec)

Standard MSI installs go through the Windows Installer service. During InstallExecuteSequence, the engine takes a single global kernel mutex named _MSIExecute.

  • Only one execute sequence holds that mutex at a time.

  • A second install does not enqueue. The API returns ERROR_INSTALL_ALREADY_RUNNING (1618), or a modal GUI says another installation is already in progress.

  • There is no public “submit install job; wake me when the mutex is free” contract for arbitrary callers.

That is serialization without a queue: exclusive, fail-closed, and opaque to agents that only see an exit code.

Custom EXE / GUI setups (Inno, NSIS, Wise, hand-rolled)

Non-MSI setup executables are not required to take _MSIExecute or any other system-wide install mutex. Unless the author opted into one, two setups can race on files (ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION), overwrite DLLs, and interleave registry writes. GUI sequences also assume a user session: HWND focus, dialogs, UAC prompts. Spawn them headless or from parallel agent workers and you get modal lockups that are not “concurrency bugs” so much as a UI model that never contemplated multiple installers as peers.

Package managers (winget, Chocolatey, Scoop)

CLI managers help humans and scripts, but they do not invent an OS job queue across independent process trees.

  • They may serialize inside their own process graph.

  • They still invoke MSIs that hit 1618, or EXE setups that ignore every global convention.

  • Failures surface as exit codes and logs—not as a durable, inspectable install queue other agents can join.

So “use winget” is necessary hygiene for agents; it is not a substitute for OS-level install concurrency design.

Why agent workflows feel this first

A single developer rarely double-clicks two setups at once. Three agent workers on one Windows desktop or self-hosted runner will:

  1. discover missing SDKs in parallel,

  2. each decide to install,

  3. each invoke winget / msiexec / a vendor EXE,

  4. and bounce—or worse, succeed into a half-corrupted tree because nothing owned the non-MSI path.

The orchestration layer must invent the queue Windows never shipped.

Workarounds that actually work today

Treat installation as a critical section owned by your agent host—not by hope.

  1. Respect _MSIExecute. Poll the mutex / Windows Installer service state before invoking msiexec; block and retry until free. This only covers MSI execute sequences.

  2. Wrap everything else in a named system mutex or file lock. One global lock for “any install this machine considers mutually exclusive”—MSI, winget, Chocolatey, custom EXE—across agent PIDs. PowerShell System.Threading.Mutex or a well-known lock file both work if every installer entrypoint cooperates.

  3. Force quiet / unattended flags inside that lock. /qn, /verysilent /norestart, winget install --silent --accept-package-agreements --accept-source-agreements, and friends. Serialization without silent mode still dies on a modal dialog nobody will click.

  4. Prefer package managers that can express intent, then still hold the outer lock while they run. Inner serialization is not enough when two agent trees each start their own manager.

None of this is elegant. It is the tax of an OS that standardized exclusion for MSI and left admission control to the ecosystem.

A feature Windows could ship (and probably will not)

The honest product ask is larger than “make 1618 wait.”

A proper install serialization API

Expose a first-class install job queue at the OS (or a privileged service) with roughly:

  • Submit — declare package identity, payload type (MSI, MSIX, declared EXE protocol, bundle), silent constraints, reboot policy, and caller identity (user, agent, MDM).

  • Observe — waitable handle / ETW / WinRT events for queued → running → succeeded/failed, with structured reasons (held by whom, estimated progress if known).

  • Policy — who may jump the queue, when reboot is allowed, whether interactive UI is permitted at all on this session.

  • Single-flight by resource — not only “one MSI execute,” but keyed exclusion for Program Files trees, service names, and driver packages when declared.

New installer builders would be required to emit against that API for Store / attestation / enterprise catalog paths—top-down pressure through WiX, InstallShield, Advanced Installer, Inno, NSIS, and the MSIX toolchain so future software conforms.

A detection and interference layer for legacy setups

Momentum and the long tail of old apps are why Microsoft will not rip out EXE setup culture tomorrow. A plausible bridge is a daemon that:

  1. recognizes common installer families (MSI engine, Inno/NSIS signatures, bootstrapper patterns, known publisher helpers),

  2. when a second install attempts mutating syscalls or reserved paths while a job is active, stalls those calls (or the relevant threads) instead of failing the whole process with a cryptic sharing violation,

  3. surfaces a user- or agent-visible notice—“Install B is waiting behind Install A”—while the stalled installer remains frozen on its blocked thread,

  4. releases the stall when the active job completes or the user/agent cancels with an explicit policy.

That is invasive. It is also the only way to give old installers queue semantics without rewriting them. Call it a feature suggestion with eyes open: enterprise antivirus and Application Control already sit near this layer; an official install serializer would need the same trust, signing, and escape hatches—and still would not cover every custom bootstrapper that writes with CreateFile and hope.

Why momentum wins

Windows cannot unilaterally redefine decades of vendor setup EXEs without breaking silent corporate images, games, OEM utilities, and every CI image that shells setup.exe /S. A clean API for new software is imaginable. A detection layer that freezes strangers’ threads is a security and compatibility minefield. So agents will keep owning the mutex for the foreseeable future—unless the package-manager and installer-builder ecosystems voluntarily converge on a shared queue protocol even without an OS mandate.

Candidate projects and their roles

Cooperation is not “everyone installs slower.” It is a shared contract: who admits work, who executes it, who declares resources, who orchestrates agents.

Project / surface Role in a working concurrency story

Windows Installer service / msiexec

Own today’s _MSIExecute truth; evolve from fail-fast mutex to queue-aware execute admission; publish waitable status beyond 1618.

MSIX / App Installer

Modern packaging path that can require declaration of install impact and reboot; natural place to attach job IDs and silent policy.

Windows Package Manager (winget)

Cross-tree client of the OS queue; stop being a second private serializer that still loses to raw msiexec and vendor EXEs; expose agent-friendly wait/stream APIs.

WiX Toolset

Authoring default for MSI/bundles that emit queue-protocol metadata and quiet-first UX; pressure point for “new software conforms.”

Inno Setup / NSIS

Dominant custom-EXE builders; must grow an opt-in (then default) “register with install serializer” stub so their runtime participates without each script reinventing mutexes.

InstallShield / Advanced Installer / InstallAware

Commercial suites that set enterprise expectations; if they adopt the API, ISVs follow; if they ignore it, the long tail never moves.

Chocolatey / Scoop

Community managers that wrap the messy EXE world; role is to hold or join the system queue, not only an internal one, and to fail with structured “queued behind …” instead of opaque exit codes.

Visual Studio Installer / channel bootstrapper

Heavy, long-running, frequently concurrent with SDK installs agents also request; must publish progress and exclusion sets other jobs can wait on.

Intune / MDM / WSUS-class deployment

Policy authority for who may install, whether UI is allowed, and reboot windows; the queue is useless if MDM and agents race underneath it.

Microsoft Defender / WDAC / App Control

Already interfere with file mutation during install; should compose with a serializer (scan without inventing a second bounce) rather than amplify ERROR_SHARING_VIOLATION.

Agent hosts (Cursor agents, Copilot coding agents, self-hosted Actions/Azure DevOps runners, etc.)

Until an OS queue exists: own the global install lock; prefer silent package-manager paths; never spawn parallel setups “because the model is multi-threaded.”

Dev-Centr Easy Installer / msi-generator

Our lane: emit silent-capable, lock-aware install entrypoints; document agent orchestration patterns; refuse to pretend a generated EXE is concurrency-safe without an outer mutex.

PowerShell DSC / configuration as code

Enterprise install orchestration; should become a first-class submitter to the queue so human MDM and agent installs share one admission path.

Cross-compose with the Linux piece

Linux already treats package databases as lockable resources and, in modern apt, can wait on those locks instead of only bouncing. That is closer to a queue’s admission behavior—but it is still per-ecosystem (dpkg vs rpm vs Flatpak), and agents still race across managers. The sibling post maps that world and lists who would need to cooperate for a cross-manager install bus.

Composition, not duplication:

  • Use this post when the failure mode is 1618, a modal “another installation is in progress,” or two EXE setups eating the same Program Files tree.

  • Use the Linux post when the failure mode is Could not get lock /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend, DNF’s transaction lock, or PackageKit vs apt on the same box.

  • Use both when designing an agent host that spans OSes: one orchestration verb (“install with exclusive machine admission”), two platform adapters, no fantasy that winget and apt already solved peer agents.

We care because Easy Installer, msi-generator, and every agentic toolchain story assume installs are boring. On Windows they are not boring—they are a single-flight problem dressed up as a desktop convenience. Until the OS grows a queue, the agent that forgets the mutex is the agent that bounces.

posts.title: Installation concurrency when Linux locks wait—or don’t
posts.description: Linux package managers serialize with lock files and, in modern apt, optional wait timeouts—but agents still bounce across dpkg, DNF, Flatpak, and GUI software centers. What exists, what to fake in orchestration, and who would need to cooperate for a real install bus.
posts.html:
Linux looks healthier than Windows at first glance: package databases have locks, distro tools know about them, and some clients can wait instead of instantly failing. That is real progress—and still not an OS-wide install queue that concurrent agent workflows can trust when one worker wants apt, another wants Flatpak, and a third is unpacking a vendor .run into /opt.

This is the Linux half of a diptych with Installation concurrency when Windows has a mutex but not a queue. Same agentic pressure; different primitives; different cooperation map.

Practitioner short form (agent-host mutex rule, no OS treatise): OS install concurrency on the docs hub.

The short answer

Linux distributions do serialize many package transactions with lock files and manager-specific transaction locks. Some stacks even wait for those locks (notably modern apt with DPkg::Lock::Timeout, and interactive apt(8) defaults). What they do not provide is a single machine-wide admission queue spanning every way software lands on disk—native packages, Flatpak/Snap, language toolchains, AppImages, and vendor install scripts—so parallel agents still bounce or race at the seams.

What actually serializes today

dpkg / apt (Debian, Ubuntu, and friends)

  • Frontend and database locks under paths like /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend and /var/lib/dpkg/lock make concurrent dpkg/apt transactions exclusive.

  • Historically, a second apt-get failed immediately with “Could not get lock …”.

  • Since apt 1.9.11-era work (widely felt on Ubuntu 20.04+), wait is a first-class option:

    • apt-get -o DPkg::Lock::Timeout=60 … waits up to N seconds; -1 waits indefinitely.

    • apt(8) itself waits by default (on the order of two minutes non-interactively, longer/infinite when interactive—treat distro docs as source of truth).

  • GUI tools (GNOME Software, Synaptic) and unattended upgrades often already waited; CLI scripts were the last to get a non-hacky story.

That is lock + optional wait for one ecosystem—not a general job queue with priorities, structured observers, or cross-manager exclusion.

RPM world (dnf, yum, zypper)

RPM-based systems take their own transaction / metadata locks. A second DNF transaction typically fails or blocks according to that stack’s rules; it does not join Debian’s locks, and it does not know about Flatpak’s. Agents that mix “install a .deb-equivalent via DNF” with “install a Flatpak” still need an outer critical section.

Arch (pacman / ALPM)

pacman holds a DB lock under /var/lib/pacman/db.lck (and related paths). Second callers fail until the lock is cleared—again, fail-or-wait is local to ALPM, not a desktop-wide install bus.

PackageKit

PackageKit’s D-Bus API was always a bid for one session/system broker above apt/dnf/zypper. In practice agents still shell out to native CLIs for determinism, and PackageKit does not own Flatpak/Snap/language toolchains as a unified queue. Treat it as an important pattern—central broker—more than a solved problem.

Flatpak, Snap, AppImage, Nix/Guix

  • Flatpak / Snap serialize their own installs/updates; they do not take dpkg locks, so they can mutate large parts of the user-visible app set while apt runs.

  • AppImage often sidesteps system package DBs entirely (file copy + desktop entry)—concurrency becomes ordinary filesystem races.

  • Nix / Guix isolate via the store; they reduce some classic shared-/usr races and introduce their own daemon/store locks. They are a different model, not a drop-in OS queue for apt-shaped workflows.

Language and vendor installers

pip, npm, cargo, SDK .run scripts, and JetBrains/Oracle-style installers do not participate in distro locks. Agents love these paths. They are exactly where “Linux has locks” becomes a false comfort.

Why agent workflows still bounce

Boot-time races are the classic demo: unattended-upgrades or cloud-init holds the dpkg lock while a provisioner runs apt-get install. Agent desktops repeat the pattern without the cloud vocabulary:

  1. Worker A installs build-essential via apt (waits correctly on dpkg).

  2. Worker B installs a Flatpak SDK and a pip tool in parallel.

  3. Worker C runs a vendor .run that writes into /usr/local.

  4. A and B “succeeded”; C raced a library; the next compile is a mystery.

Linux gave us better intra-manager manners than Windows MSI’s fail-fast 1618. It did not give agents a cross-manager single-flight guarantee.

Workarounds that actually work today

  1. Prefer wait over poll hacks for apt. Use DPkg::Lock::Timeout (or apt(8)’s built-in wait) instead of fuser loops when you are in the Debian family.

  2. Hold an outer orchestration lock anyway. One named mutex / flock that covers “any mutating install this host considers exclusive”—apt, dnf, flatpak, snap, vendor .run—across agent PIDs. Distro locks are necessary; they are not sufficient.

  3. Serialize privilege prompts. polkit / sudo password storms from parallel agents are a human denial-of-service. Batch installs under one elevated session or a pre-authorized policy.

  4. Know your GUI neighbors. GNOME Software and Discover may already own the PackageKit/apt lock; agents should wait, not kill, those transactions.

  5. Prefer declarative store models when the workload allows. Nix-style isolation shrinks shared mutable /usr—at the cost of teaching agents a different install verb.

A feature Linux could grow (without pretending systemd can wish away apt)

Linux does not need a Windows-style “freeze stranger threads in CreateFile” daemon as badly—lock files and D-Bus brokers are already the culture. The missing piece is a cross-manager install bus with teeth:

Machine-wide install admission

A privileged service (evolving PackageKit, or a leaner successor) that:

  • accepts jobs from apt/dnf/pacman backends, Flatpak/Snap, and a declared “foreign installer” protocol for vendor scripts,

  • provides waitable job handles for agents (sd-bus / varlink / simple CLI),

  • publishes who holds what (pkg DB, user Flatpak installation, /opt/vendor) without scraping lsof,

  • supports timeouts, cancel, and reboot inhibit composition with systemd-inhibit.

Optional syscall stall for foreign installers

Vendor .run and AppImage “install to /opt” flows will never all rewrite for the bus. A small compatibility shim—eBPF or LSM-hook based admission that delays write opens under protected prefixes while a job is active, and notifies the user/agent—is the Linux rhyme to the Windows detection-layer idea. It should be opt-in/enterprise-profile, not a surprise for every desktop: freezing writers is still a compatibility weapon.

Distros will not “force” every ISV tomorrow any more than Microsoft will. They can make the bus the default path for Software centers, cloud-init, and fleet agents—and shame raw parallel apt-get in root CI images the way they already shame curling bash into prod.

Candidate projects and their roles

Project / surface Role in a working concurrency story

dpkg / apt

Own Debian-family DB locks; keep improving wait defaults and machine-readable “blocked on pid …” output for agents; integrate as a backend to a shared bus rather than only a private lock file.

RPM / dnf / yum / zypper

Same role on RPM distros: transaction locks that can be observed and waited on by a broker; structured conflict reasons agents can parse.

pacman / ALPM

Arch’s lock owner; needs the same observe/wait story when agents and AUR helpers race.

PackageKit

Existing D-Bus broker pattern; strongest candidate to become the cross-backend admission queue if clients stop bypassing it for “real” work.

Flatpak / Snap

Parallel app runtimes that must join system admission when they mutate shared OS integration (MIME, PATH helpers, system helpers)—not only their own repos.

GNOME Software / KDE Discover / Apper

Human-facing queue UI; should display agent jobs and vice versa so the desktop does not feel haunted when automation installs.

unattended-upgrades / cloud-init

Boot and maintenance holders of locks; must publish long-running job identity so agents wait with context instead of timing out blindly.

systemd (systemd-inhibit, transactional update stories)

Reboot/shutdown inhibit and (where used) transactional roots; compose with install jobs so “install finished” and “safe to reboot” are one timeline.

polkit

Authorization for who may submit install jobs; stop parallel password prompts from becoming the concurrency failure mode.

Nix / Guix

Alternate isolation model; role is interoperability notes (when store installs still touch profiles/user envs that conflict with apt-world agents).

Homebrew on Linux / language package managers

High-churn agent paths; should either stay in user trees without claiming system locks, or explicitly take the outer install flock when they touch shared prefixes.

Ansible / Puppet / Salt / fleet agents

Classic orchestrators; should submit to the bus (or hold the outer flock) so human Software Center and CI agents do not fight config management.

Coding / desktop agents (Cursor agents, Copilot agents, runner sidecars)

Consumers: one “install exclusively” adapter per host; prefer apt wait options; never assume Flatpak and apt are free to overlap.

Dev-Centr Easy Installer (Linux plugins / AppImage path)

Our lane: emit entrypoints that honor distro locks and an outer agent flock; document when AppImage/portable PATH installs are the concurrency escape hatch.

Cross-compose with the Windows piece

Windows standardized a global MSI execute mutex and almost nothing else—then taught a generation of tools to fail with 1618. Linux standardized per-database lock files and slowly taught apt to wait. Neither OS gives agents a complete answer when “install” means five different package universes.

Composition:

  • Windows post — feature ask leans toward a new serialization API plus a legacy detection/stall layer, because custom EXE culture never shared a lock file convention.

  • This post — feature ask leans toward strengthening a PackageKit-shaped bus and optional LSM/eBPF admission for foreign writers, because lock-and-wait is already native vocabulary.

  • Shared orchestration rule — until those exist, agents own a host-wide install critical section on both platforms; silent/unattended flags; one admission owner per machine.

If your failure mentions _MSIExecute or “Another installation is already in progress,” start with the Windows essay. If it mentions lock-frontend, DNF’s transaction lock, or Software Center vs apt, you are here. If you are writing an agent host, you need both adapters—and the humility to treat “install” as scheduled work, not a fire-and-forget side effect of a clever model.

posts.title: Why Git feels hard when features aren’t files
posts.description: Git stores file blobs, not features or dependencies. That is why unrelated functions collide on pull, and why connectome-fs (now under Dev-Centr) treats semantic units and graph edges as filesystem-native.
posts.html:
We transferred connectome-fs into the Dev-Centr org and wrote up a thesis that usually lives in a personal essay: Git feels difficult because it will not admit that features are not files.

The epiphany in one paragraph

You cannot honestly commit two unrelated features that happen to share a file as two first-class histories—only as hunks you babysit. Git also does not know that api.ts depends on auth.ts. So when Alice lands a typo fix and Bob is editing a different function in the same path, Bob still pays the stash → pull → unstash tax and may eat a conflict for a system he never touched.

That meta-information—units of change, dependency edges, “this patch is safe to broadcast”—is exactly the kind of thing a graph / dependency filesystem should own. Unison proves the point from the language side with content-addressed definitions. Connectome-fs aims at the substrate: GUID nodes, associations, editions, and eventually syntax-aware auto-forward for boring fixes.

Where to read it

  • Practitioner essay (docs hub): Git’s file-shaped change model

  • Canonical design (connectome-fs): Semantic change units

  • Sibling concurrency thread: Git concurrency enshittification — many live trees; this post is about the wrong unit inside a tree

  • Repo: dev-centr/connectome-fs

posts.title: When code platforms flatten portfolios
posts.description: GitHub spent the word Projects on boards, not on nesting product families under a portfolio. A short Dev-Centr note on forge ontology — with the HCI essay as the deeper cut.
posts.html:
We keep stuffing systems work into the wrong GitHub containers because the forge never modeled the hierarchy people already use: portfolio → charter org → product → repos → working sets.

GitHub’s Projects are boards and tables. They are not projects in the human sense — coordinated bodies of work with many assets under a brand. So maintainers invent nesting with org-owned orgs, personal dumps, or bloated “devtools” houses that absorb an operating-system trajectory by accident.

That is a schema and UX failure, not a personal branding problem.

The deeper cut lives on HCI-Nerdz — where product representation and cognitive tax belong:

When forges lack super-orgs

Why Dev-Centr is commenting

We run a Development Orchestration Suite. We are not the natural owner of a filesystem substrate, even when git concurrency and agent workspaces desperately want one. connectome-fs now lives under github.com/connectome-fs so systems adapters, demos, and drivers can accumulate without rewriting Dev-Centr’s charter every quarter.

Practical rule for our catalog:

  • Dev-Centr — orchestration, installers, agent hosts, practitioner docs

  • Partner systems orgs — substrates and runtimes with their own gravity

  • Cross-link aggressively — do not merge charters to save a URL

Until forges grow a real super-org / product-family type, that rule is how we stop paying the flatten tax.

posts.title: Business Bootstrap becomes a support-systems hub
posts.description: Founder ops docs grow past email—scheduling, design, and vaults get their own capability areas on docs.devcentr.org.
posts.html:
Business Bootstrap on docs.devcentr.org is no longer just the email matrix and org infra pattern. It is a support-systems hub: Email, Scheduling, Design, Vault, and Org infra—each with room for explanation, how-tos, and interconnect notes.

What landed first under the new shape:

  • Scheduling — Cal.com (hosted) vs Cal.diy (MIT self-host)

  • Design — Penpot as the open canvas default; Figma when partners already live there

  • Vault — Bitwarden cloud vs official self-host vs Vaultwarden

The stack map and stage defaults stitch the areas together. Product partner marketplaces stay elsewhere; this hub is for the IT skeleton every tech company ends up building anyway.

Start at the hub index or the stack map.

posts.title: MSI tables land in the generator
posts.description: msi-generator v0.2 writes real OLE2 compound files, cabinets, and core Windows Installer tables — still unsigned, no longer an empty stub.
posts.html:
msi-generator crossed the line from “skeleton that prints a message” to “file you can open in an OLE/MSI viewer.”

v0.2 writes a version-3 compound file, an uncompressed cabinet payload, and the core table set (Directory, Component, File, Feature, FeatureComponents, Property, Media, plus _Tables / _Columns and the string pool). MSIX gained multi-file payloads and placeholder assets so manifests stop lying about missing logos.

This is the engine Easy Installer’s msi / msix plugins call. It is not WiX, and we are not pretending a unsigned sample MSI is Store-ready — but the binary formats are finally real enough to iterate on.

Release: v0.2.0 · docs: component.

posts.title: Easy Installer becomes Ibex
posts.description: Install Builder EXtension — new name, logo, and OS package registries for the installer-authoring CLI.
posts.html:
Easy Installer is now Ibex (Install Builder EXtension): same job — author installer packages, emit CI, and put tools on PATH — clearer name, animal mark, and first-class installs via winget / Homebrew / Scoop.

  • CLI: ibex (v0.2 dual-ships transitional easy-installer-* release assets)

  • Install: winget install DevCentr.Ibex · brew tap dev-centr/tap && brew install ibex

  • Docs: Ibex · repo still dev-centr/easy-installer for now

Not a software catalog installer — it extends file managers and DevCentr; it does not replace winget for installing third-party apps.

posts.title: Easy Installer ships
posts.description: A CLI and Explorer menu for installer projects and Install in-place PATH — without waiting on a full MSI every time you want a tool on PATH.
posts.html:
We shipped Easy Installer: the host that turns “put this folder on PATH” and “build an installer from this tree” into something you can right-click or script.

The first beat is deliberately small. Install in-place (add to PATH) means what it says — append the folder to the user PATH, keep a ledger so you can undo, and skip the copy-into-Program-Files ritual when you are iterating on a CLI. File Explorer gets a menu for it (Win11 modern when the sparse package builds; classic cascade otherwise). Linux and macOS get file-manager actions too.

The second beat is the project file. installer.kdl plus plugins: portable zip always works; NSIS and Inno emit scripts and call their compilers when present; MSI/MSIX call msi-generator; AppImage gets a stub path on Linux. Optional designer GUIs are discoverable (plugins install-gui) instead of reinvented inside our IDE.

DevCentr picks up the same verbs — New → Installer Project, toolbar Install in-place PATH, and CLI modes — so the OS menu and the app are not two products pretending to be one.

Docs: Easy Installer (once the hub rebuilds) · releases.

Figure 1. Idealized Easy Installer project UI
Figure 2. DevCentr extension surface

posts.title: Easy Installer emits CI pipelines
posts.description: Scaffold GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines, Jenkins, CircleCI, or Bitbucket workflows for installer builds — without packaging on your laptop.
posts.html:
Easy Installer now has a first-class CI pipeline intent: edit ci-runner.sdl, run emit-ci, and get runner YAML plus CI-INSTALLER.adoc (how to enable pipelines, secrets, tags, and artifact downloads). Local build stays optional for smoke tests.

Supported emitters in this cut: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines, Jenkins (Declarative), CircleCI, and Bitbucket Pipelines. DevCentr’s New Installer dialog can choose CI pipeline only; Explorer gets New Installer CI pipeline… (--mode=emit-ci).

Docs: emit CI how-to · repo.

posts.title: We’re partnering with OpenShellOrg (on purpose)
posts.description: DevCentr and OpenShellOrg are locking in the sibling story—toolchain ownership on our side, shell entrypoint honesty on theirs.
posts.html:
Quick confession: for a minute we almost convinced ourselves the whole “wrong Node / wrong Flutter / wrong host” rant lived under OpenShellOrg, because that’s where the pain hits—you type a command and the wrong process runs. Then we remembered why we put Toolchain Management in DevCentr in the first place: the full lifecycle (pin, health, repair, upgrade) is an ecosystem-orchestration problem. The shell just happens to be the crime scene.

So we’re doing the grown-up thing.

DevCentr keeps the canonical Toolchain Management Pattern → Protocol → Control Plane → TCF kit. That’s the “official entrypoint owns the lifecycle” philosophy, the advisories in Ecosystem Management, the “stop telling newcomers to go shop for nvm/FVM first” stance.

OpenShellOrg keeps the shell-boundary essay: Entrypoint Dispatch — auto-install and re-exec the right host/version when the pin says so — plus nu-require, SOS, structured-shell thesis, env-refresh / shell-host plans. Complementary. Not a duplicate manifesto with a different logo.

Aligned, not merged. Cross-linked like we mean it. Footers and org profiles now show the sibling cluster so people stop spelunking.

If you want the vibe in one line: we orchestrate the workshop; they refuse to let the hammer lie about which nail it’s hitting.

Figure 1. Official toolchain architecture
Figure 2. Sibling ownership

Links worth bookmarking: OpenShellOrg, their docs, Toolchain Management Pattern, and the alignment page in general-knowledge (Dev-Centr and OpenShellOrg).

posts.title: We’re opening a News desk
posts.description: Why DevCentr is starting a public News feed—and what you won't find here.
posts.html:
Dev-Centr has been shipping in public for a while—docs, tools, the app, the whole messy orbit of related projects. What we haven’t had is a place to talk about that work like people talk about it: the why, the bets, the “here’s where we’re headed” pieces.

So we’re starting News at devcentr.org/news.

Think magazine column more than release notes. If something changes how we build, how we show up as an org, or what we’re trying to become, it belongs here. If it’s “we fixed a heading and renamed three pages,” that’s the Changelog.

We’ll write when there’s something worth saying. No weekly quota. No content mill. Subscribe to the RSS or Atom feed if you want a ping when we do.

Elsewhere, as always: the docs, the repos, and the app.

posts.title: Stop dumping people into the docs
posts.description: We built a Help hub so “I need assistance” doesn't mean “go read the manual.”
posts.html:
Here’s a quiet failure mode a lot of open projects share: someone shows up stuck, and the only door we offer is documentation. Docs are great when you want to learn. They’re a cold shoulder when you want a person—or at least a clear path to one.

So we put up a Help hub at devcentr.org/help.

The idea is simple. Help is the umbrella. Under it you can choose self-help (docs, guides, the knowledge base) or support (talk to us). Status and community channels sit next to both, so you’re not hunting through the footer for Slack or “is the site up?”

We don’t have a polished ticket desk yet—and we’re not going to pretend we do. For now, mail support@devcentr.org. A real assisted desk (tickets, maybe AI triage) is on the roadmap; we’d rather ship an honest front door than a half-built system with a shiny button.

If you just want the pulse of our public surfaces, /status runs live probes. Longer uptime history still lives at status.devcentr.org.

This is a small change on the site. It’s a bigger change in posture: we assume visitors arrive with different jobs to do, and we stop treating “read the docs” as the only answer.

posts.title: Our logo shouldn’t need a proprietary player
posts.description: Why DevCentr's new mark stays in SVG—and why we're cautious about Rive as a default for open brands.
posts.html:
We finally gave DevCentr a proper mark: an orbital hub that reads as a center of gravity. You’ll see it on the site, in the GitHub avatar, and in the motion loop that doesn’t need JavaScript to breathe.

That last part matters more than it sounds.

There’s a loud fashion in product design right now: ship brand motion as a black-box file, drop in a player, call it modern. Rive is genuinely good at interactive chrome—state machines, theme hooks, the works. Its runtimes are open. The editor isn’t, and the .riv format is binary. That means weak git diffs and a hard wall for anyone (human or agent) who wants to edit the motion as text.

We’re building an open ecosystem. Our logo shouldn’t be the one asset that only opens in a paid app.

So the default for portable marks stays animated SVG and CSS. Lottie when you’ve got a baked After Effects timeline. Rive when you’re already deep in interactive app UI and the player is justified. We’re documenting those lanes in General Knowledge; the short version is: don’t hard-advocate a proprietary editor as the open standard for brand motion.

Longer term we want something text-first that agents can actually edit. Popkorn is an early CSS-shaped candidate—interesting, not a Dev-Centr default yet. If that future interests you, there’s an open thread on rich interactivity at ayarse/popkorn#7.

The mark is the visible change. The opinion underneath it is the story: open brands should travel as open source.
